rows.title: NuclearLang in the editors — Why
rows.summary: Why
body: - Write, run, debug, call the API and hand work to agents in one place, not a terminal per task.
- The same diagnostics, completion and colors in every editor.
- No language or dialect logic in an extension: that is `nuclear-lsp` and the dialects' data.

rows.summary: A project is checked with the dialect its manifest names.
body: A project is checked with the dialect its manifest names. `nuclear.dialectPaths` adds folders with dialects, and
`<workspace>/dialects` is always searched. Zed passes `lsp.nuclear-lsp.settings` as `{ nuclear: ... }`.

rows.summary: The server is `nuclear-lsp`, built from `nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp` (`cargo build --release -p nuclear-lsp` at the tree's root → `target/release/nuclear-lsp`).

the tree's root → `target/release/nuclear-lsp`). Each extension runs it as an external binary. Its modules and its

rows.title: How an extension finds the language server — The bundle of VS Code and JetBrains
rows.summary: `vscode/scripts/bundle-server.mjs` (`npm run server`) and `jetbrains/build.sh` build the server and copy, next to it: definitions; a dialect's `docs/` stays behind) (`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/`) Both end with `nuclear-lsp --check-bundle`, which loads each bundled dialect without the…
body: `vscode/scripts/bundle-server.mjs` (`npm run server`) and `jetbrains/build.sh` build the server and copy, next to
it:
- `server/nuclear-lsp`
- `server/dialects/`: every dialect of the tree (`nuclearlang/dialects/`, each language with its frameworks and type
definitions; a dialect's `docs/` stays behind)
- `server/platforms/<platform>/platform.toml`: the contract of each platform
(`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/`)
Both end with `nuclear-lsp --check-bundle`, which loads each bundled dialect without the tree and fails on any
error (N0213, for example); a warning (a platform plugin a dialect does not bring yet) is printed and does not fail. The server finds the dialects next to its binary; it also searches
`nuclear_dialect::install_dir()` (the installed copy).

rows.title: How an extension finds the language server — The server's life
rows.summary: stdin closes.
body: - VS Code stops the server 5 minutes after the last `.nuc` closes (`watchIdle`); the server also exits when its
stdin closes.
- The JetBrains IDE manages the server's process itself.

rows.title: How an extension finds the language server — Where each one looks, in order
rows.summary: Zed has no bundle: its server is the one `installer/install.sh` installs, which finds its dialects and type definitions in `share/nuclearlang`.
body: | Editor | Order | Code |

| VS Code | the setting `nuclear.server.path` → `server/nuclear-lsp` inside the extension → a development build beside the extension (`../target/release`, then `../target/debug`) → the `PATH` | `findServer` in `vscode/src/extension.ts` |
| Android Studio / IntelliJ | *Settings → Tools → NuclearLang* (server path) → `server/nuclear-lsp` inside the plugin → the `PATH` | `NuclearSettings.findServer` |
| Zed | `lsp.nuclear-lsp.binary.path` → the `PATH` → `~/.local/bin/nuclear-lsp` | `zed/src/lib.rs` |
Zed has no bundle: its server is the one `installer/install.sh` installs, which finds its dialects and type
definitions in `share/nuclearlang`.

rows.title: Architecture of the editor tooling — Code metrics
rows.summary: A faithful copy of the CodeMetrics extension (the user asked for the same messages): the same setting names, default costs and English texts.
body: A faithful copy of the CodeMetrics extension (the user asked for the same messages): the same setting names, default
costs and English texts. They are computed in the server; a client shows the list
(`nuclear.showCodeMetricsCodeLensInfo`) and the colors (`nuclear/codeMetrics`, or the command `nuclear.codeMetrics`
in JetBrains). For a client whose `clientInfo.name` starts with `Zed` the server answers the list with

(`vscode/scripts/codemetrics-settings.mjs` from `nuclear-lsp --codemetrics-defaults`): never edit
`nuclear.codemetrics.*` by hand. Credits: `vscode/THIRD-PARTY.md`.

| File of the project | Written by | Read by |

| `.nuclear/project.json` (the project card: platform, dialect, output folder, toolchain; [projects §1.1](../../../nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/projects.md)) | the server (`Project::build`) and the CLIs | the VS Code status bar, the workspace, the tools |

rows.title: Architecture of the editor tooling — What the three share
rows.summary: All of it lives in `vscode/` and is generated or copied for the other two (a sibling extension that is not there is skipped): VS Code, JetBrains and Zed; Zed's icon themes come from `zed/scripts/icons.mjs` over `vscode/icon-themes` (the theme).
body: All of it lives in `vscode/` and is generated or copied for the other two (a sibling extension that is not there is
skipped):
- **Themes and icons**: `vscode/theme/` (`palette.json`, `build.mjs`, `icons.mjs`) writes the Chernobyl themes of
VS Code, JetBrains and Zed; Zed's icon themes come from `zed/scripts/icons.mjs` over `vscode/icon-themes`
([the theme](../../vscode/docs/02-architecture/theme.md)).
- **The TextMate grammar**: `vscode/syntaxes/nuclear.tmLanguage.json`, also packed by `jetbrains/build.sh` (without
the `@example` patterns) and copied by the website. Zed has its own tree-sitter grammar.
- **The language configuration**: `vscode/language-configuration.json` (comments, pairs, `offSide` folding,
`onEnterRules` for ` * `); JetBrains packs it without `onEnterRules`, Zed repeats its indentation rules.
- **The code metrics settings**: generated from the server's defaults.

rows.title: The Synapsis device (`mobile-device.ts`) — The page in the panel
rows.summary: `attach` opens the extension's own CDP connection (over node's WebSocket): input lands where it is drawn.
body: `attach` opens the extension's own CDP connection (over node's WebSocket):
- **`emulate`**: metrics, touch and user agent of the preset, so Flutter behaves as on iOS or Android and every
input lands where it is drawn. The first time it is a `Page.navigate` already emulated; later a `Page.reload`,
only if the platform changes.
- **The screencast**: `Page.startScreencast` (also on `Page.loadEventFired`), jpeg 100, at `r.density` = the
physical pixels the panel shows the screen at. The webview reports `shot` = CSS width × zoom × `devicePixelRatio`
in its `size` message; `sized` sets `density = max(dpr, shot / width)`, capped at 4, and only ever raises it,
emulating again. Before the first measurement it falls back to `captureScale(p)`. So a frame matches the device's
on-screen pixels 1:1 and nothing is upscaled (a 2x cap, and even the full `dpr`, blurred phones zoomed on a HiDPI
screen).
- **Input**: `Input.dispatchTouchEvent` / `MouseEvent` / `KeyEvent`.
- It reconnects (`cdp.onclose`, 10 tries) and emulates again when a frame's size differs (every 2 s at most).
- `closeBrowser` at the end.

rows.title: Architecture of the devices — Hiding, parking, ending
rows.summary: `watchdog()` runs every `WATCH_MS` (one minute): it ends the idle devices and, with `pgrep -af` by marker, reaps the keys no app owns.
body: | What happens | Effect |
| The user closes a device's tab | the disposed panel parks its app: it goes on, hidden; the Devices pane lists it (`hidden:<key>` ids) and `revealDevice` adopts it again |
| The workspace switches tab (`Workspace.switchTabs`) | `nuclear.parkDevices` → `DevicePanel.park()`: the panels close, the apps go on with their sessions (`parked`) |

| A mobile workspace or the Devices tool is entered | `nuclear.unparkDevices` → `unpark()`, after the code is reopened: each device gets a fresh locked editor group to the right of the code (`lockDeviceGroup`), never merged into the code's group |
| ✕ of the Devices pane (`nuclear.closeDevice(id)`), the panel's ■, the end of its session | `endRunning`: the session, the CDP connection, the browser and `reap` |
| A parked app's session ends | cleaned by `endRunning` |
| Nobody looked at a device for `IDLE_LIMIT` (30 minutes: hidden, or its panel not visible) | the watchdog ends it |
`watchdog()` runs every `WATCH_MS` (one minute): it ends the idle devices and, with `pgrep -af` by marker, reaps
the keys no app owns.

rows.title: Architecture of the devices — Panels and running apps
rows.summary: panels' apps + `parked`.
body: - `panels` is a `Set<DevicePanel>`; each has its own `running`, `lastView` and `id`.
- `Running` (an app) lives on its own: `panel` is optional, with `title`, `lastUsed`, `ended`. `alive()` = the
panels' apps + `parked`.
- `DevicePanel.show(context, preset?)` always opens one more panel (title `Synapsis device N`; a `preset` message
selects the device). `freeNumber()` gives the lowest free number, so a closed device frees its name.
- The launch configuration carries `synapsisPanel`, the panel to run on, and its `name` is the device's title (the
debug toolbar and the Debug Console pick by device). `nuclear.runOnDevice(panelId?, root?, noDebug)`: without a
panel it takes `DevicePanel.idle()`, a free panel, or a new one. A running device is never replaced.
- `watchSessions` finds the panel of a session by `running.key`.
- `devices()` / `devicesChanged` / `revealDevice` feed the workspace's Devices pane.

- `marker(key)` = `__synapsis_device_<extension host pid>_<key>__`, written in `--web-launch-url`, so every
process of a device carries it.
- `reap(mark, wait?)` is a detached `sh`: it waits for `wait` to die, then `pkill -TERM -f`, 3 s, `-KILL`. On
activation one is left waiting for the extension host itself, so a closed or crashed VS Code ends every app the
window started; a device that ends reaps its own key. There is no Windows version.

session, so you can run two signed-in users of a chat side by side. A device takes the lowest free number
(`Synapsis device 1`, `2`…). The debug sessions carry its name.

What happens to a device:
| You… | The device |
| close its tab | is hidden: the app goes on, and the Devices tool shows it again |
| switch to a project tab that is not mobile, or to another tool | is parked, and comes back when you return to a mobile project or the Devices tool |
| press ✕ in the Devices tool or ■ in the panel, or its session ends | ends now |
| do not look at it for 30 minutes | ends by itself |
| close VS Code, or VS Code crashes | ends, with its `flutter run` and its browser |
A watchdog checks every minute and ends any Flutter or browser process the window no longer owns.

rows.title: Architecture of HTTP Connections — A component's panel (`panel.ts`)
rows.summary: `ComponentPanel`: one webview panel per `componentKey(endpoint)`, like a Bruno folder, with an inner tab per endpoint opened from the tree.
body: `ComponentPanel`: one webview panel per `componentKey(endpoint)`, like a Bruno folder, with an inner tab per
endpoint opened from the tree. Each inner tab keeps its request and its last response:
- the method, the url with its path and query parameters, the headers, the body (with the sample);
- send: by the extension host with `fetch`, a 30 s timeout, the active environment's variables and headers;
- the response pretty-printed; *copy as curl*.
The webview posts its whole state (`tabs`, `active`) on every change and the model keeps it in `memory` by key, so
`restore(keys)` rebuilds the panels when the HTTP Connections workspace is entered again (`model.reopen` = the keys open when
it was left). The memory lives in the window, not on disk.

`{ "id": 1, "method": "GET", "path": "/tasks/{id}", "headers": {}, "body": … }` (a full HTTP request through the app,
so its guards and validation answer as over HTTP), an event as `{ "subscribe": "tasks.created" }` and

rows.title: Architecture of HTTP Connections — The contract it reads for WebSockets
rows.summary: A backend's contract says what its WebSocket serves (ADR-synapsis-0008, ADR-synapsis-0007; the format: projects §1.2).
body: A backend's contract says what its WebSocket serves (ADR-synapsis-0008, ADR-synapsis-0007; the format:
[projects §1.2](../../../../../nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/projects.md)). Each field may be absent, and then the
endpoint is HTTP only (an older contract shows as it did).
| Field | Meaning | What the tool does with it |
| `webSocket` | the path of the app's socket (`"/ws"`), or `null` | the socket's url: the base url plus this path; no events without it |
| `controllers.<C>.transports` | `["http"]` or `["http", "websocket"]` | `websocket`: the routes carry the `WS` badge |

| `guards`, `controllers.<C>.guards` | the app's guards, then the controller's: `{"guard": "token", "header": …}`, `{"guard": "noOrigin"}` | each token's header is proposed (`{{token}}`; `Bearer {{token}}` in `Authorization`, the default header) |
| `events.<topic>` | the `component` that publishes it, its `payload` and the map's `fields` | an `EVENT` row under that component |

`ws::` panels too, which come back with their sockets closed.

rows.summary: only your `.nuc`, at full speed.
body: - A debugger stops the app; a profiler of the target shows the generated code and its libraries. The monitor shows
only your `.nuc`, at full speed.

the app runs ──► NuclearMonitor writes the report every 2 s while something changed, and at exit
FileSystemWatcher **/.nuclear/monitor/report.json ──► MonitorPanel.refresh ──► nuclear monitor --json ──► page()
- `readMonitor` runs `nuclear monitor --json --project <folder>` from the active `.nuc`'s folder (or the first
folder of the workspace); the command finds the report there or above. Without a report the page shows the
command's message and how to get one.
- The tree: one `<details>` per node, open for the first two levels and for every flagged node; the bar's length is
the node's time against the longest root, its darker part the own time. Concurrent children can add up past

project is the folder above `.nuclear/`).
- Redraws are debounced (300 ms): the app writes at most every two seconds.

rows.title: Nuclear Monitor
rows.summary: 1. Run your app with the monitor: `nuclear run --monitor` (a backend), or `nuclear build --monitor` and run it your usual way (a program of Node.js, Python or Dart).
body: 1. Run your app with the monitor: `nuclear run --monitor` (a backend), or `nuclear build --monitor` and run it your
usual way (a program of Node.js, Python or Dart). Use it: open the screens, call the routes that are slow.
2. In VS Code run *Nuclear: Open Monitor* (with a `.nuc` of the project open). In a terminal: `nuclear monitor`.
3. Read the **hot spots** first:
- `slow`: its own time is a fifth or more of the whole call;
- `async calls in a loop`: an async call made five or more times, one after another, inside one call of its
parent: start them together (`~awaitAll([...])`);
- `many connections`: ten or more new connections per call (a client or a pool made per call);
- `much memory`: 10 MB or more grown per call.
4. Open the tree under a hot spot: each row is a function with its time (the bar; its own time darker), calls,
connections and memory. Click a name to open its `.nuc` at the line.
A save in the editor builds the project again without the monitor: measure, then edit.
Build again without `--monitor` before you ship: the monitor is for finding the problem, not for production.
What it cannot do yet: a phone or a browser tab cannot write the report to your project's folder (the
[roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md)).

rows.title: VS Code extension — Rules
rows.summary: `server/`, `out/`, and the `nuclear.codemetrics.*` settings of `package.json`.
body: - Never edit what is generated: `themes/`, `icon-themes/`, `icons/`, `syntaxes/nuclear-example.tmLanguage.json`,
`server/`, `out/`, and the `nuclear.codemetrics.*` settings of `package.json`.
- The engines have no `vscode` import, so a node script and the tests drive them: the tools' `runs.ts`,
`support.ts`, `workbench.ts`, `cdp.ts`, `web-session.ts`, and `src/chatHost.ts`. Keep it so.
- The set-up of the AI services is `nuclear-builder setup` (Nuclear, `../tools/nuclear-builder/`), run as a
process (`aiMachine.ts`): the extension never re-implements it.
- A page is only a view. A Nuclear Builder run or a chat job belongs to the extension (module-level), so closing
its page or switching tools leaves the work running.
- An installer runs in a terminal the user sees, never hidden.
- A tool is documented in `../tools/<tool>/`, not here.
- After a change, release: [`../docs/06-runbooks/release.md`](../docs/06-runbooks/release.md). The user must quit
VS Code completely to see a changed theme.

body: - **Breakpoints in the `.nuc`**: click the gutter of a `.nuc`. The extension puts a mirror breakpoint on the
matching line of the generated file, which is the one the debugger stops on. The `.nuc` breakpoint can stay
"unverified": that is expected. Conditions and logpoints work too. The mirrors move after each build.
- **The paused line**: on each pause the `.nuc` opens with the line highlighted, to the left of the generated
file (`nuclear.debug.followInNuclear`).
- **Step by Nuclear line**: `F10`, `F11` and `Shift+F11` step until the pause is on another `.nuc` line or in
another call. They apply when the pause is in code that comes from a `.nuc` and the focus is on a `.nuc` (or the
pause came from a `.nuc` breakpoint). The debug toolbar has a *Step Over (Nuclear Line)* button, and the usual
buttons still step in the generated code.
- **Values**: hover a name in the `.nuc` to see its value. With `debug.inlineValues` on, each local variable's
value shows at the end of its line.
- **Nuclear Call Stack**: a view in the Run and Debug panel while paused in a `.nuc`. Each frame opens at its
`.nuc` line, or at the generated file for library code.
- **Go to the Same Line in Nuclear / Dart** (the editor's context menu while debugging): jumps from the `.nuc` to
the generated file and back.

rows.title: Run, debug and tasks in VS Code — Debugging a `.nuc`
rows.summary: Problems panel.
body: - **Run-time errors (Dart only)**: an exception, or an error Flutter prints, is marked on its `.nuc` line in the
Problems panel. A panel *Nuclear: runtime error* opens beside it with the explanation of `nuclear explain`, the
stack in Nuclear and the original Dart error (`nuclear.debug.explainErrors`). The next build clears the mark.
Some names Dart writes differently cannot be seen by their Nuclear name: the parameters of a `stateful` are
`widget.x`, and Dart's reserved words are escaped.

**F5 with no `launch.json`** (the debugger *Synapsis (Flutter app)*). Each one runs `nuclear build` and launches
the `<project> (debug)` configuration on the device you pick. The build's output goes to the *Synapsis* output
panel.
- **Hot reload on save**: with the app running, `Ctrl+S` on a `.nuc` builds and hot reloads it. If Flutter rejects
the reload, the extension does a hot restart.
- **Repair**: when the build fails, the app ends before it starts (and you did not stop it), or a reload gives a
Dart compile error, the extension runs `nuclear repair` and launches the app again. It does this once per launch;
after that it only reports the failure.
- The first time the app is created with the window already open, accept **Reload Window**, so the Dart
extension finds the app.

([the devices](../../../tools/nuclear-device-manager/docs/08-guides/README.md)).

body: - **The `.nuc` never bends to Dart.** Names are written as they are: Nuclear's `camelCase` is Dart's.
- **Nothing of Dart or Flutter in Rust.** Generic mechanisms belong in the compiler (projects, `decor`,

contract first; `frameworks/flutter/` adds how it is written in Dart (ADR-dart-0001).
- The generated code is what an expert would write: `const` constructors, no layer that adds nothing at run time;
it passes `flutter analyze` without warnings.
- The automatic imports of the SDK and of the packages come from the type definitions (`[dialect] defs`), not from
hand-written lists. An `[auto_imports]` entry exists only for a package without definitions (`fpdart`, the test
libraries) or to choose the module of a name two packages export.

rows.summary: template variable (the language project decides it), never as a case of one language.
body: - **The `.nuc` never bends to TypeScript.** Names are written as they are: Nuclear's `camelCase` is TypeScript's.

contract first, for every dialect of the platform; `frameworks/<name>/` adds how it is written in TypeScript.
- The generated code passes `tsc --strict`.
- The order of `defs` in a framework dialect decides which package gives a name two of them export: change it only
knowing which name moves.
- [`nodejs`](../nodejs/AGENTS.md) sits between this dialect and `nestjs` and is postponed by the user: do not
touch it until asked.
- `docs/07-reference/*.md` hold only final rules and real equivalences (`spec-check`, 0 problems). Never edit an
equivalence by hand: change the dialect, then `--fix` and review.

rows.title: The Zed extension: its files — The grammar (`grammar/`)
rows.summary: A tree-sitter grammar of tokens: comments, strings with `${}`, numbers, decorators, words, operators and nested brackets.
body: A tree-sitter grammar of tokens: comments, strings with `${}`, numbers, decorators, words, operators and nested

rows.title: NuclearLang for Zed — Tasks and the ▷ in the gutter
rows.summary: The two *Nuclear:* tasks always pass `--dialect flutter`.
body: *task: spawn* (`alt-shift-t`) lists the tasks. Run them from any `.nuc` of a project.
| Task | What it runs |
| Nuclear: generated code of *file* | `nuclear build <file> --dialect flutter`: prints the generated code |
| Nuclear: check *file* | `nuclear check <file> --dialect flutter` |
| Synapsis: run (r = hot reload, R = hot restart) | `nuclear run`, in a new terminal |
| Synapsis: device (own window, like an emulator) | `nuclear device` |
| Synapsis: terminal device (inside this terminal) | `nuclear terminal-device` |
| Synapsis: build | `nuclear build` |
| Synapsis: watch (build on every save) | `nuclear watch` |
| Synapsis: test | `nuclear test` |
| Synapsis: test "*name*" | `nuclear test -- --plain-name "<name>"` |
| Synapsis: analyze | `nuclear analyze` |
| Synapsis: repair | `nuclear repair` |
| Synapsis: explain the error in the clipboard | the clipboard (`wl-paste` or `xclip`) into `nuclear explain` |
The two *Nuclear:* tasks always pass `--dialect flutter`.
In the gutter, ▷ next to `main(` offers run, device and terminal device. ▷ next to each `@test`, `@widget` or
`@states("name")` runs only that test.
To see a change in a running app, start **watch** and **run**, then press `r` in the run terminal.

rows.title: NuclearLang for Zed — Turn on the features
rows.summary: By default Zed turns off the server's semantic tokens, outline, folding and code lenses.
body: By default Zed turns off the server's semantic tokens, outline, folding and code lenses. Turn them on in
`settings.json`:
```json
"code_lens": "on",
"languages": {
"Nuclear": { "semantic_tokens": "combined", "document_symbols": "on", "document_folding_ranges": "on" }
The server gives diagnostics, quick fixes, completion, hover, signature help, go to definition, references, rename,
outline, folding and the colors by meaning. A click on a code metrics lens shows the details as a message.

rows.title: NuclearLang for Zed — What Zed does not allow
rows.summary: Zed gives an extension no panels, views, keybindings or actions on save.
body: Zed gives an extension no panels, views, keybindings or actions on save. So there is no Synapsis device inside the
editor (`nuclear device` opens its own window), no `.nuc` breakpoints or debugging, no build and hot reload on
save, no automatic repair, no generated code view beside the file and no Nuclear workspace. Nuclear Builder and
HTTP Connections are not offered in Zed. They are in [VS Code](../../../vscode/docs/08-guides/README.md).
